Abstract A significant increase in circulating cell‐free DNA (cfDNA) occurs with physical exercise, which depends on the type of exertion and the duration. The aims of this study were as follows: (1) to investigate the time course of cfDNA and conventional markers of muscle damage from immediately after to 96 h after muscle‐damaging exercise; and (2) to investigate the relationship between cfDNA and indicators of primary (low‐frequency fatigue and maximal voluntary isometric contraction) and secondary (creatine kinase and delayed‐onset muscle soreness) muscle damage in young healthy males. Fourteen participants (age, 22 ± 2 years; weight, 84.4 ± 11.2 kg; height, 184.0 ± 7.4 cm) performed 50 intermittent drop jumps at 20 s intervals. We measured cfDNA and creatine kinase concentrations, maximal voluntary isometric contraction torque, low‐frequency fatigue and delayed‐onset muscle soreness before and at several time points up to 96 h after exercise. Plasma cfDNA levels increased from immediately postexercise until 72 h postexercise ( P < 0.01). Elevation of postexercise cfDNA was correlated with both more pronounced low‐frequency fatigue ( r = −0.52, P = 3.4 × 10 −11 ) and delayed‐onset muscle soreness ( r = 0.32, P = 0.00019). Levels of cfDNA change in response to severe primary and secondary muscle damage after exercise. Levels of cfDNA exhibit a stronger correlation with variables related to primary muscle damage than to secondary muscle damage, suggesting that cfDNA is a more sensitive marker of acute loss of muscle function than of secondary inflammation or damaged muscle fibres. What is the central question of this study? How do plasma cell‐free DNA (cfDNA) levels change in response to primary and secondary muscle damage when muscle‐damaging exercise is performed without metabolic stress? What is the main finding and its importance? In this study, we found that cfDNA concentration increases following severe primary and secondary muscle damage after 50 drop jumps. However, acute postexercise increases in cfDNA were higher than following secondary muscle damage and were more correlated with variables related to primary muscle damage (low‐frequency fatigue). This suggests that muscle‐damaging exercise causing no accumulation of metabolites can lead to acute and delayed increases in cfDNA levels. Experimental Physiology , 109 , 1341 – 1352 . 10.1113/EP091986 Handling Editor: Toby Mundel 1 INTRODUCTION Performing unaccustomed exercise can lead to muscle damage, especially when muscles perform eccentric contractions (Chalchat et al., 2022 ). In contrast to concentric or isometric contractions, eccentric lengthening contractions cause more profound sarcomere damage that leads to a more severe inflammatory response (Markus et al., 2021 ). Drop jumps (DJs) are a very common plyometric exercise used in sports training that are eccentrically biased. They are also one of the most powerful tools for the examination of exercise‐induced muscle damage (Dias et al., 2022 ; Tanabe et al., 2022 ). Mechanically demanding contractions, particularly those in muscles unaccustomed to eccentric contractions (Dargeviciute et al., 2013 ; Newham et al., 1987 ), such as those used in DJs, can result in disruption of muscle‐fibre structure, protein leakage, prolonged force depression, delayed‐onset muscle soreness (DOMS) and inflammation (Clarkson & Hubal, 2002 ; Peake et al., 2017 ). Several markers describe these changes in sports science; however, the mechanisms by which they function or are released are highly distinct. Increases in plasma biomarkers, such as creatine kinase (CK), C‐reactive protein or myoglobin, are often used to evaluate the magnitude of exercise‐induced muscle damage (Dias et al., 2022 ; Dupuy et al., 2018 ). However, there has been much debate in the last few years about the use of CK, e.g., owing to its slow reaction time and declining response to increased training levels, which, in turn, decrease its sensitivity to changes in training load (Haller et al., 2023 ; Saw et al., 2016 ). Previous studies have suggested reduced muscle force after eccentric exercise as the most appropriate indirect marker (Damas et al., 2016 ; Paulsen et al., 2012 ). However, the relationship between levels of circulating muscle‐specific proteins (myoglobin and CK) and muscle function appears to be inconsistent (Friden & Lieber, 2001 ). As an example, loss of force and CK activity have different time courses. Muanjai et al. ( 2019 ) reported that a decrease in force and a rise in CK levels represent different types of muscle damage, termed primary and secondary, respectively. Low‐frequency fatigue (LFF; the ratio of forces generated at 20 and 100 Hz stimulation), which is attributable to decreased sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca 2+ release and/or diminished myofibrillar Ca 2+ sensitivity, in addition to an increase in reactive oxygen species, can also be used as an indirect marker of primary damage (Wyckelsma et al., 2020 ). Secondary damage results in structural changes to the muscle fibre. Furthermore, damage might be attributable to white blood cell infiltration (mainly neutrophil granulocytes) of the muscle or increased intracellular Ca 2+ activating phospholipase and protease enzymes (Yamada et al., 2018 ). Neither of the discussed markers (CK or LFF) is sensitive enough to respond to both acute exercise and secondary muscle damage, making alternative biomarkers necessary. Cell‐free DNA (cfDNA), which is DNA released from cells that circulate in the bloodstream, could potentially serve as a substitute marker for exercise‐induced muscle damage (Andreatta et al., 2018 ). Cell‐free DNA is known to be a pro‐inflammatory load‐dependent marker of aerobic and anaerobic exercise (Breitbach et al., 2012 ; Huminska‐Lisowska et al., 2021 ). An increase in the level of this marker is associated with the activation and recruitment of immune cells (Korabecna et al., 2020 ). In healthy individuals, exercise is the primary external variable contributing to increased cfDNA levels (Andreatta et al., 2018 ; Atamaniuk et al., 2010 ; Haller et al., 2017 ). Many of the published studies have used protocols that require muscles to perform concentric and eccentric contractions, such as cycling (Tug et al., 2017 ), aerobic running (Haller et al., 2017 ), marathon (Atamaniuk et al., 2008 ) or lifting exercise (Atamaniuk et al., 2010 ), and light and heavy resistance training (Andreatta et al., 2018 ), meaning that simultaneous metabolic stress (accumulation of metabolites, i.e., lactate, H + ions in muscle cells and altered calcium homeostasis) and mechanical stress (structural changes involving sarcomere, cytoskeletal and membrane damage; disruption of excitation–contraction coupling) would occur. Only one study focused solely on eccentric training, where high‐intensity and low‐intensity eccentric cycling exercise was compared (Mavropalias et al., 2021 ). Although the protocol involved eccentric exercise, the participants performed high‐intensity cycling, in which the accumulation of metabolites would have been present but lower than that of exercise in most previous studies (Juškevičiūtė et al., 2023 ; Tug et al., 2017 ). Hence, the extent to which the increase in cfDNA is caused by mechanically demanding exercise alone is unclear. To our knowledge, no studies have investigated the effects of DJs on cfDNA concentrations. In the present study, we wanted to observe how mechanically demanding exercise, without placing the organism under metabolic stress, affects cfDNA levels. It was thought that muscle contraction without the accumulation of metabolites, such as lactate, could increase cfDNA levels, first, because of physical exertion and, second, because of neutrophil infiltration into tissues owing to local inflammation and oxidative stress (Mortaz et al., 2018 ), because neutrophils are essential in the release of cfDNA (Moss et al., 2018 ). Here, we aimed to examine the time course of plasma cfDNA levels after intermittent DJs and assess the extent to which cfDNA increases in the absence of metabolic stress. We also analysed whether plasma cfDNA levels change in response to DOMS and levels of CK, and whether there are associations between plasma cfDNA levels and neuromuscular fatigue indices. We aimed to test the hypothesis that cfDNA reacts to acute exercise (primary damage), in addition to delayed muscle damage (secondary damage).

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the time course of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) and conventional muscle damage markers in response to mechanically demanding muscle-damaging drop jump exercise without significant metabolic stress in healthy males. It found that cfDNA levels increased acutely and with a delayed response up to 72 hours post-exercise, correlating strongly with primary muscle damage indicators (low-frequency fatigue, MVIC torque, P20/P100 torque) and delayed-onset muscle soreness. This suggests cfDNA is a sensitive marker for acute loss of muscle function after mechanical stress, offering insights into primary and secondary muscle damage responses.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Fourteen participants performed 50 intermittent drop jumps once, from heights of approximately 0.5 m (ranging from 30.37 ± 5.55 cm to 36.39 ± 6.83 cm) with 20-second rest intervals between each jump. This protocol was designed to be mechanically demanding, inducing sufficient primary and secondary muscle damage, without placing the organism under significant metabolic stress. No dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels increased acutely from 0.97 ± 0.19 to 1.5 ± 0.21 ng/mL (log10 scale, P < 0.01) immediately post-exercise, normalizing by 90 min. Significant delayed increases were also observed after 6 h (1.25 ± 0.25 ng/mL, P < 0.01), 12 h (1.29 ± 0.27 ng/mL, P < 0.01), 48 h (1.26 ± 0.41 ng/mL, P < 0.05), and 72 h (1.42 ± 0.55 ng/mL, P < 0.01), recovering by 96 h. Moderate increases (approximately 5-fold) were noted.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Circulating nucleic acids released from cells into the bloodstream, reflecting cell injury/death (passive release) or active cellular secretion; involved in aseptic inflammatory responses and immune cell activation. It is a pro-inflammatory, load-dependent marker.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Muscle-damaging exercise (50 intermittent drop jumps) performed without significant metabolic stress; changes in response to severe primary and secondary muscle damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A sensitive and comprehensive marker for acute loss of muscle function (primary muscle damage) and secondary muscle damage. The initial elevation likely reflects primary muscle damage, while secondary increases may indicate local inflammation. Significantly correlated with LFF (r = -0.52, P = 3.4 × 10^-11), P20 torque (r = -0.45, P = 4.8 × 10^-8), P100 torque (r = -0.3, P = 0.00038), MVIC torque (r = -0.29, P = 0.00048), and DOMS (r = 0.32, P = 0.00019).

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased from 2.22 ± 0.29 to 2.31 ± 0.24 IU/L (log10 scale) at 90 min post-exercise (P < 0.05), to 2.62 ± 0.26 IU/L at 6 h post-exercise (P < 0.001), and peaked at 12 h post-exercise (2.77 ± 0.28 IU/L, log10 scale, P < 0.001). Levels did not return to baseline by the end of the experiment (96 hours).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An enzyme involved in energy metabolism within muscle cells; its presence in plasma indicates muscle cell membrane integrity disruption, typically linked to secondary muscle damage (structural changes to muscle fibers).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: After muscle-damaging drop jump exercise, peaking at 12 hours post-exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A widely accepted marker of muscle damage, but showed no significant correlation with cfDNA or LFF in this study, suggesting a poor relationship with functional outcomes. It represents secondary muscle damage.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased to 61.3% ± 15.3% (P < 0.0001) immediately after 50 DJs; not fully recovered by 48 h (88.4% ± 13.0%, P > 0.05 compared to pre-exercise values). Elevation of post-exercise cfDNA was correlated with more pronounced LFF (r = -0.52, P = 3.4 × 10^-11).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicates a specific type of muscle fatigue often linked to structural disturbances within muscle fibers, attributable to decreased sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release, diminished myofibrillar Ca2+ sensitivity, and increased reactive oxygen species, reflecting primary muscle damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Immediately and up to 48 hours after 50 Drop Jumps (mechanically demanding exercise).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle damage and impaired muscle function, with mechanically induced LFF generally caused by structural disturbances within muscle fibers. Negatively correlated with cfDNA, suggesting a link between cfDNA and the severity of LFF (primary muscle damage).

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased to 83.1% ± 5.75% directly after exercise (P < 0.001); progressively restored to baseline values over the recovery period. cfDNA was correlated with MVIC torque (r = -0.29, P = 0.00048).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measures the maximum force-generating capacity of a muscle under voluntary contraction; an indicator of primary muscle damage and acute loss of muscle function.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Immediately after 50 Drop Jumps (mechanically demanding exercise).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle impairment and serves as an indirect indicator of the severity of skeletal muscle damage, potentially reflecting muscular impairment rather than neuronal activity impairment.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Peaked at 1-2 days post-exercise; 4.31 ± 1.65 at 24 h (P < 0.05) and 4.31 ± 2.50 at 48 h (P < 0.05). Six participants reported soreness (1-2 on a scale from 0 to 10) at 96 h (1.77 ± 1.79), not statistically significant compared to pre-exercise. Elevation of post-exercise cfDNA was correlated with DOMS (r = 0.32, P = 0.00019).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Perception of muscle pain and discomfort, indicative of delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), linked to inflammatory response and structural muscle damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following muscle-damaging drop jump exercise, peaking at 1-2 days post-exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of secondary muscle damage and inflammatory response; showed a significant moderate positive correlation with cfDNA levels, where higher cfDNA was associated with greater soreness.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Slight decrease immediately after exercise (94.1% ± 5.76%, P < 0.05), 45 min post-exercise (93.8% ± 7.21%, P < 0.05), and 90 min post-exercise (90.7% ± 8.77%, P < 0.05), but restored after 6 h (P > 0.05).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects the ability of the central nervous system to maximally activate a muscle.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Slight impairment suggests muscular impairment rather than a significant decrease in neuronal activation following the exercise.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly decreased post-exercise (49.7% ± 17.8%, P < 0.001) compared with the pre-exercise value (100%); recovered only at 72 h after exercise (92.5% ± 15.0%, P > 0.05). Correlated with cfDNA (r = -0.45, P = 4.8 × 10^-8).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measures the force response of a muscle to a low-frequency electrical stimulation, reflecting contractile properties and fatigue.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle fatigue and damage caused by the experimental exercise, with prolonged recovery.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased due to DJs (79.5% ± 15.4%, P < 0.01); restored at 12 h after exercise (91.9% ± 10.6%, P > 0.05). Correlated with cfDNA (r = -0.3, P = 0.00038).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measures the force response of a muscle to a high-frequency electrical stimulation, reflecting contractile properties and fatigue.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle fatigue and damage caused by the experimental exercise, with restoration within 12 hours.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significant decrease immediately post-exercise (from 1.52 ± 0.29 to 1.21 ± 0.35 mmol/L, P = 0.016); decrease still evident 45 min post-exercise (1.2 ± 0.28 mmol/L, P = 0.012).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A byproduct of anaerobic glycolysis, typically indicating metabolic stress, but also used as a substrate for energy production.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Immediately and 45 minutes post-exercise after 50 Drop Jumps (exercise designed to be without metabolic stress).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: The observed decrease confirms that the exercise protocol did not induce significant metabolic stress and suggests accelerated lactate uptake and utilization by muscles, rather than accumulation.
